claims.text: Strength and deformation behavior in multi-component concentrated alloys are primarily governed by lattice distortion induced by atomic size mismatch.
Atomic size mismatch can be systematically varied while other influential variables are held as constant as possible.
Lattice distortion can be assessed through X-ray diffraction peak broadening.
Electron microscopy can be used to assess local strain fields associated with lattice distortion.
Increasing atomic size mismatch creates greater lattice distortion.
Greater lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion produces higher yield strength.
Alloys with higher atomic size mismatch will have greater yield strength than baseline alloys with minimal mismatch.
Alloys with higher atomic size mismatch will have lower ductility than baseline alloys with minimal mismatch.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold when the alloys retain a stable, predominantly single-phase homogeneous microstructure.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold when impurity effects are minimal and processing and testing conditions are identical.
The proposed relationship may not hold outside moderate temperature ranges.
Electronic effects or short-range order may govern deformation strongly enough to invalidate the proposed size-mismatch relationship.
Failure to observe a statistically significant strength increase, accompanying lattice distortion, and corresponding ductility changes in the high-mismatch series would falsify the hypothesis.
